planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to a half day of sun; Aphrodite needs more warmth and light than most hostas to flower reliably and often takes a season or two to settle in before blooming heavily.

directions: Aphrodite is a rare double-flowered form of the fragrant plantain lily, bearing glossy, rounded apple-green leaves and clusters of pure white, rose-like double blooms that open in late summer and fill the evening air with a strong, sweet scent. Because it flowers on new growth produced late in the season, it wants more warmth and a bit more sun than typical shade hostas, and cool climates with a short growing season may see it bloom sparingly. It is slower to establish and multiply than most modern hybrids, so gardeners are encouraged to be patient rather than divide it too soon. Site it near a patio, walkway, or open window where its powerful fragrance can be enjoyed on summer evenings.

common_name: Lemon Lime Hosta (Miniature Chartreuse-Gold Edging Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions or small container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Lemon Lime forms a dense miniature mound and is commonly used as a fast, inexpensive edging or rock-garden hosta.

directions: Lemon Lime is one of the most widely propagated small hostas in the nursery trade, forming a low, tight mound of narrow, glossy chartreuse-to-gold leaves that brighten quickly in spring. Pale lavender, narrowly funnel-shaped flowers appear on slender scapes held just above the foliage in summer. Its small mature size and fast multiplication rate make it a dependable, budget-friendly choice for edging shaded paths, tucking into rock gardens, or massing as a groundcover under trees. Give it a bit of morning light to keep the color vivid, since deep shade can dull the chartreuse cast toward plain green.

common_name: Twilight Hosta (Blue-Green Hosta with Creamy Gold Margin)

planting.note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Twilight arose as a sport of Halcyon and holds its blue cast best out of direct afternoon sun.

directions: Twilight is a sport of the popular blue hosta Halcyon, keeping its parent's frosty blue-green leaf color at the center but adding an irregular, brightening margin of creamy yellow that pales toward white as the season progresses. Near-white, bell-shaped flowers rise on scapes above the mounded foliage in mid-summer. Its wavy leaf margins and two-tone coloring give it strong presence as a specimen or accent plant even at moderate size, and it multiplies at a steady, manageable pace. Keep it out of hot midday sun, which can fade both the blue center and the gold edge.

common_name: Tortilla Chip Hosta (Miniature Rippled Gold Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some morning sun; Tortilla Chip needs enough light to color up gold but not so much that its thin, heavily rippled leaves scorch.

directions: Tortilla Chip is a miniature gold hosta named for its thin, intensely rippled and twisted leaf surface, which curls and puckers dramatically as the leaves mature through the season. Pale lavender flowers appear on short scapes held just above the compact mound in summer. Its small scale and bold texture make it a favorite for containers, rock gardens, and the front of a shaded border where its unusual leaf form can be appreciated up close. Provide a bit of morning sun to intensify the gold coloring, but shield it from hot afternoon exposure that can scorch the thin leaf substance.

common_name: Northern Exposure Hosta (Blue-Green Hosta with Wide Cream Margin)

planting.note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Northern Exposure is a large sport of Krossa Regal and needs ample room to reach its full mature spread.

directions: Northern Exposure is a large-leaved sport of Krossa Regal, keeping its parent's substantial, upright, vase-shaped habit and thick blue-green leaf substance while adding a wide, irregular creamy-white margin. Near-white flowers rise well above the foliage on tall scapes in summer. Its heavy leaf substance offers good resistance to slug damage compared with thinner-leaved hostas, and its large mature size makes it an effective focal point in a shaded border or foundation planting. Give it plenty of room to develop its full vase-shaped clump, since crowding neighboring plants can flatten its naturally upright form.

common_name: Ground Master Hosta (Vigorous Spreading White-Margined Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, average garden soil in partial to full shade; Ground Master spreads steadily by rhizome and is grown commercially as a fast, low-maintenance shaded groundcover.

directions: Ground Master is a fast-spreading, wavy-leaved hosta long used in commercial and municipal landscaping as a dependable shaded groundcover rather than a specimen plant. Its medium-green leaves are edged in an irregular band of creamy white, and the clump spreads steadily by rhizome to knit together into a dense, weed-suppressing mat within a few seasons. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer, though the plant is valued chiefly for its spreading habit and reliable coverage. It tolerates a wider range of soil and light conditions than most named specimen cultivars, making it a practical choice for large-scale shaded plantings.

common_name: Golden Meadows Hosta (Gold-Centered Hosta with Green Margin)

planting.note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade with a little morning sun; Golden Meadows is a sport of June and colors best with some light rather than deep shade.

directions: Golden Meadows is a sport of the widely grown June hosta, carrying a broad, bright gold-to-chartreuse center with an irregular dark-green margin, a brighter and more expansive gold pattern than its well-known parent. Lavender flowers appear on scapes above the mounded foliage in summer. Its center coloring shifts through the season, emerging chartreuse-gold in spring and deepening as temperatures rise, giving the clump changing seasonal interest. A little morning sun helps intensify the gold center, while afternoon shade prevents the margins from scorching.

common_name: Lakeside Cameo Hosta (Miniature Variegated Lakeside Series Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Lakeside Cameo is a miniature Lakeside series selection best sited where its small-scale variegation can be viewed up close.

directions: Lakeside Cameo is a miniature selection from the extensive Lakeside breeding series, forming a small, tidy mound of rounded, heart-shaped leaves variegated with irregular creamy-white centers against a green margin. Lavender flowers appear on short scapes just above the foliage in summer. Its diminutive scale suits container culture, rock gardens, and the front edge of a shaded border, where larger cultivars would quickly overwhelm it. Keep it consistently moist, since small hostas with less leaf mass to store moisture dry out and stress faster than large-leaved types during hot spells.

common_name: Designer Genes Hosta (Twisted Rippled Deep Green Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Designer Genes produces heavily twisted, narrow leaves and looks best planted where its unusual texture can be seen at close range.

directions: Designer Genes is grown for its unusual leaf form rather than variegation, producing narrow, deep-green leaves that twist, ripple, and curl along their length in a dense, textural mound. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer, though the distorted, glossy foliage is the main ornamental draw. Its compact size and bold texture make it a good conversation-piece specimen for containers or the front of a shaded bed planted alongside smoother-leaved companions for contrast. Consistent moisture and steady feeding help the plant fill out its dense, curled foliage mass each season.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Hyacinthina is an old, exceptionally vigorous fortunei selection that bulks up quickly into a full clump.

directions: Hyacinthina is one of the classic Hosta fortunei selections long grown in Western gardens, forming a dense, symmetrical mound of gray-green leaves that mature to a soft blue-green as the season progresses. Its pale lavender, funnel-shaped flowers are held well above the foliage on tall, upright scapes in early to mid-summer, a trait that has earned it long-standing recognition among older hosta cultivars. It is exceptionally vigorous and shade-tolerant, multiplying steadily into a full-size clump within a few seasons even in less-than-ideal soil. Its reliability and long garden history make it a benchmark blue-green hosta against which newer cultivars are often compared.

common_name: Fortunei Aurea Hosta (Spring Gold Fortune's Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some morning sun; Fortunei Aurea emerges brightest gold in cool spring weather and fades toward chartreuse-green as summer heat arrives.

directions: Fortunei Aurea is a long-established gold-leaved selection of Hosta fortunei, unfurling bright yellow-gold in spring before gradually fading toward a softer chartreuse-green as summer temperatures rise, a seasonal color shift typical of many older gold hosta cultivars. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes above the mounded foliage in mid-summer. Its early, vivid spring color makes it a useful companion for spring bulbs and emerging woodland perennials before summer shade fully closes in. A little morning sun deepens and prolongs the gold coloring, while hot afternoon exposure can scorch the leaves.

common_name: Montana Aureomarginata Hosta (Glossy Green Hosta with Gold Margin)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Montana Aureomarginata is a large, vigorous cultivar and needs ample room to display its full mature clump.

directions: Montana Aureomarginata is a large, vigorous cultivar of the robust Hosta montana, bearing glossy, deeply veined dark-green leaves edged in an irregular band of bright gold-yellow that is brightest on newly emerging spring foliage. White flowers appear on tall, sturdy scapes in early summer, earlier than many other hosta cultivars. Its bold scale and strong garden presence make it well suited to anchoring a large shaded border or woodland planting where smaller hostas would be lost. Give it generous spacing, since crowded plants lose the clean, upright form that shows off its glossy, gold-rimmed foliage.

common_name: Tokudama Aureonebulosa Hosta (Blue-Green Hosta with Gold Cloud Center)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Aureonebulosa is a slow-growing classic tokudama form best given a few extra seasons to reach full size.

directions: Aureonebulosa is a classic variegated form of Hosta tokudama, bearing thick, heavily corrugated, cupped blue-green leaves with an irregular, cloud-like center variegation of yellow-gold that gives the cultivar its name. Near-white flowers appear on short scapes largely hidden within the foliage in early summer. Like other tokudama forms it is naturally slower to grow and multiply than many modern hybrids, rewarding patient gardeners with an especially thick-textured, slug-resistant clump over time. Its compact, rounded habit and heavy substance suit it well to a prominent spot in a shaded rock garden or specimen bed.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Marginato-alba is an older, somewhat less vigorous cultivar and benefits from richer soil than many modern fortunei hybrids.

directions: Marginato-alba is one of the earliest hosta cultivars described in Western horticulture, forming a modest mound of oval, gray-green leaves edged in a narrow, crisp white margin. Pale lavender flowers appear on upright scapes above the foliage in mid-summer. It is somewhat less vigorous and more prone to summer leaf browning at the white margin than many modern hybrids, so it appreciates consistently moist soil and a bit more shelter from afternoon sun. Its historic status makes it of particular interest to hosta collectors tracing the origins of variegated fortunei-type cultivars in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in average, moist garden soil in partial to full shade; Erromena is an unusually adaptable, vigorous form of undulata tolerant of drier soil and more sun than most hostas.

directions: Erromena is an all-green, larger-leaved form within the Hosta undulata complex, lacking the white-streaked variegation of its better-known sibling cultivars but exceeding them in vigor and garden toughness. Its glossy, wavy-margined leaves form a full, rounded mound, and pale lavender flowers rise on tall scapes well above the foliage in mid-summer. Because it tolerates drier soil and more sun exposure than most hostas without losing form, it has long been used as sturdy filler and understock in mixed shaded plantings. Its rapid multiplication rate makes it an economical choice for quickly covering ground in a new shaded border.
